sla_notes_intro: Agriculture is the science and practice of growing crops and rearing animals for food, raw materials and income.
sla_notes_details: The branches of agriculture include crop production (agronomy and horticulture), animal production, soil science, agricultural economics, agricultural engineering, fisheries (aquaculture), forestry and agribusiness. Agriculture is important because it provides food, employment, raw materials for industries, foreign exchange from export crops and income for households. It relates to Biology (plant and animal life), Chemistry (fertilisers and soil), Geography (climate and soils), Mathematics (measurements and records) and Business Studies (marketing and accounts).
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a farmer who grows tomatoes (crop production), keeps chickens (animal production) and sells the produce in the market uses several branches of agriculture together.
sla_notes_daily_life: Agriculture employs most Tanzanians and supplies food, so knowledge of it supports both household food security and self-employment.
sla_exercise: Define agriculture.::The growing of crops and rearing of animals for food, raw materials and income.||Name three branches of agriculture.::Crop production, animal production and agricultural economics.||Give two importance of agriculture.::It provides food and employment.

sla_notes_intro: Soil is the loose upper layer of the earth's crust in which plants grow, made of weathered rock, organic matter, air, water and living organisms.
sla_notes_details: Soil forms through weathering of parent rock by physical (temperature changes, water, wind), chemical (oxidation, hydrolysis, carbonation) and biological (plant roots, organisms) processes, together with addition of humus. The factors of soil formation are parent material, climate, living organisms, topography and time. Physical properties include texture (sand, silt, clay), structure, porosity, colour and water holding capacity; chemical properties include pH, nutrients and cation exchange capacity; biological properties include soil organisms such as earthworms, bacteria and fungi.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, sandy soil drains quickly and holds few nutrients, while clay soil holds water and nutrients but drains slowly; loam, a mixture of sand, silt and clay, is best for most crops.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers test soil texture and pH to choose crops and decide whether to apply lime, manure or fertiliser.
sla_exercise: Name the three soil particles by size.::Sand, silt and clay.||Give two factors of soil formation.::Parent material and climate (or living organisms, topography, time).||Which soil type is ideal for most crops?::Loam soil.

sla_notes_intro: Horticultural crops are vegetable, fruit and flower crops grown intensively on small areas.
sla_notes_details: Principles and practices include site selection, land preparation, nursery establishment and raising of seedlings (tomato, onion, Chinese cabbage) or direct sowing (amaranth), transplanting, spacing, mulching, watering, weeding, fertiliser or manure application, pest and disease control, harvesting, post-harvest handling and marketing. Good practices depend on crop requirements for soil, temperature and moisture.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, tomato seedlings are raised in a nursery for about four weeks then transplanted to the field at a spacing of about 60 cm by 45 cm.
sla_notes_daily_life: Vegetable production provides quick income to households and supplies nutritious food to markets and schools.
sla_exercise: Name two horticultural crops.::Tomato and onion (or amaranth, Chinese cabbage).||Why are seedlings transplanted?::To establish healthy plants that will grow strongly in the field.||State one post-harvest practice.::Grading and packing (or cooling, storage).

sla_notes_intro: Poultry production is the rearing of birds such as chickens and ducks for meat, eggs and income.
sla_notes_details: Types of chicken are layers (eggs), broilers (meat) and dual purpose (eggs and meat); ducks are also raised. Principles and practices include housing (ventilation, space, litter), feeding using balanced rations, provision of clean water, brooding of chicks, vaccination and disease control (such as Newcastle disease), biosecurity, record keeping, egg handling and marketing.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, chicks need brooding at about 32 to 35 degrees Celsius in the first week, and a layer flock should be vaccinated against Newcastle disease according to schedule.
sla_notes_daily_life: Poultry keeping is a quick source of protein and income for many rural and urban families.
sla_exercise: Name the three types of chicken by use.::Layers, broilers and dual purpose.||Why are chicks brooded?::To keep them warm until they can regulate their body temperature.||Give one disease control practice in poultry.::Vaccination (or biosecurity).

sla_notes_intro: Husbandry practices are the day-to-day activities carried out on crops from land preparation to harvest.
sla_notes_details: Students practise preparing beds, raising nurseries, sowing and transplanting amaranth, Chinese cabbage, onion and tomato, applying manure, watering, mulching, staking (tomato), weeding, controlling pests and diseases, harvesting, and keeping records of inputs, labour and yields. Safe use of tools and protective clothing is observed.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a class prepares a 2 m by 5 m bed, adds well-decomposed manure, transplants tomato seedlings and records growth each week.
sla_notes_daily_life: Practical skills gained help students start small vegetable gardens at home or in the community.
sla_exercise: Why is mulching done?::To reduce water loss and suppress weeds.||Name one tool used to prepare a nursery bed.::Hand hoe (or rake, spade).||Why keep production records?::To calculate costs, yield and profit.

sla_notes_intro: Poultry husbandry practices are the routine tasks needed to keep birds healthy and productive.
sla_notes_details: Practices include cleaning and disinfecting the house, preparing litter, brooding chicks, feeding using feeders and drinking using drinkers, vaccination, deworming, controlling external parasites, culling, egg collection and grading, and record keeping for mortality, feed consumption and egg production. Local, layer, broiler and dual-purpose chickens and ducks are managed according to their needs.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, feed is provided in clean feeders and water in drinkers, and dead or sick birds are removed immediately to prevent disease spread.
sla_notes_daily_life: These practices are directly applicable to running a small poultry business.
sla_exercise: Name two poultry equipment.::Feeders and drinkers.||Why is litter changed or turned regularly?::To keep the house dry and reduce disease and ammonia.||What records are kept in a layer unit?::Egg production, feed consumption and mortality.

sla_notes_intro: Banana and root, stem and tuber crops such as cassava, sweet potatoes and round (Irish) potatoes are important food and cash crops.
sla_notes_details: Bananas are propagated by suckers or tissue culture plantlets, planted in holes with manure at a spacing of about 3 m by 3 m, and managed by mulching, de-suckering, desurfacing, weeding, pest control (weevils) and disease control (Panama disease, black sigatoka). Cassava is propagated by stem cuttings, sweet potato by vine cuttings and round potato by seed tubers. Practices include land preparation, planting, weeding, ridging, fertiliser or manure use, pest and disease control, harvesting and storage.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, cassava stem cuttings of about 25 cm with at least five nodes are planted at 1 m by 1 m and are ready for harvest at 9 to 18 months depending on variety.
sla_notes_daily_life: These crops are staple foods in many regions of Tanzania and also give income from sales.
sla_exercise: How is cassava propagated?::By stem cuttings.||Name one banana pest.::Banana weevil.||How is round potato propagated?::By seed tubers.

sla_notes_intro: Pigs and rabbits are small livestock that give meat and income from small spaces.
sla_notes_details: For pigs, principles include selection of breeds, housing with adequate space, feeding using balanced rations, breeding and farrowing management, and health control (vaccination, deworming and control of African swine fever through biosecurity). For rabbits, cages or hutches, feeding with hay, vegetables and pellets, breeding at about 5 to 6 months, kindling management and disease control are important. Both need clean water and proper waste handling.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a sow has a gestation period of about 114 days (three months, three weeks and three days), and a doe rabbit about 30 days.
sla_notes_daily_life: Rabbit and pig keeping are good projects for families with limited land and for school clubs.
sla_exercise: What is the gestation period of a rabbit?::About 30 days.||Name one disease that affects pigs.::African swine fever.||Why should rabbit hutches be raised above the ground?::To keep them dry and protect the rabbits from predators and disease.

sla_notes_intro: Cereals such as maize, sorghum and paddy (rice) and pulses such as beans, cowpeas and pigeon peas are major food crops.
sla_notes_details: Practices include selecting suitable varieties, land preparation, timely planting at recommended spacing, use of certified seeds, fertiliser or manure, weeding, pest and disease control (stalk borers, armyworms, rust), crop rotation and intercropping with legumes, harvesting, drying, storage and marketing. Pulses fix nitrogen in the soil and improve fertility. Rice may be grown under rain-fed or irrigated conditions.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, maize is spaced at 75 cm between rows and 25 cm between plants, and intercropping maize with beans makes good use of land and improves soil nitrogen.
sla_notes_daily_life: Cereals and pulses are staples for food security, and surplus sales bring income to farmers.
sla_exercise: Why are pulses important in crop rotation?::They fix nitrogen and improve soil fertility.||Name two cereals.::Maize and sorghum (or paddy).||Give one storage pest of grain.::Weevil (or larger grain borer).

sla_notes_intro: Cattle are kept for milk (dairy), meat (beef), manure and draught power.
sla_notes_details: Principles include choosing suitable breeds (for example Friesian and Ayrshire for dairy, Boran for beef), housing, feeding with pasture, fodder and concentrates, water provision, breeding and calf rearing, milking practices, disease and tick control (East Coast fever, foot and mouth disease), dipping or spraying, record keeping and marketing.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a dairy cow needs about 3 to 4 percent of her body weight in dry matter daily and plenty of clean water to produce milk.
sla_notes_daily_life: Cattle keeping contributes to household income, nutrition and rural livelihoods.
sla_exercise: Name one dairy breed.::Friesian (or Ayrshire).||Why are cattle dipped?::To control ticks and tick-borne diseases.||Give two products from cattle.::Milk and meat.

sla_notes_details: Practices include choosing suitable varieties, land preparation, planting at correct spacing and depth, fertiliser or manure use, weeding, pest and disease control (for example rosette in groundnut), harvesting at maturity, drying, shelling, storage and marketing. Groundnut, a legume, fixes nitrogen; sunflower and simsim are rotated with cereals.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, groundnut is sown about 45 cm between rows and 10 to 15 cm within rows and harvested when the leaves turn yellow.

sla_notes_intro: Aquaculture is the farming of aquatic organisms such as fish, sea cucumbers and seaweed in controlled environments.
sla_notes_details: Principles include site selection, pond or cage design, water quality management (temperature, oxygen, pH), stocking of fingerlings, feeding, growth monitoring, disease control, harvesting and marketing. Common fish are tilapia and catfish; sea cucumber and seaweed farming are done in coastal waters. Aquaculture reduces pressure on wild fish stocks.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, tilapia fingerlings are stocked in a well-prepared pond at a recommended density and fed daily with a balanced feed.
sla_notes_daily_life: Fish farming provides protein and income, especially near lakes, rivers and the coast.
sla_exercise: Name one fish commonly farmed in ponds.::Tilapia (or catfish).||Why is water quality monitored?::Poor water quality can reduce growth or kill fish.||Name a seaweed or marine aquaculture product.::Seaweed (or sea cucumber).

sla_notes_details: Practical tasks include preparing land, planting at recommended spacing, thinning, weeding, pest and disease control, top-dressing where needed, harvesting, threshing or shelling, drying, storing and recording yields and costs.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, sunflower is harvested when the back of the head turns yellow-brown and the seeds are dry.
sla_notes_daily_life: The practical skills can be used to increase production of oil seeds at home.
sla_exercise: When is sunflower ready for harvest?::When the back of the head turns yellow-brown and seeds are dry.||Why weed a crop early?::To reduce competition for water, light and nutrients.||What is shelling?::Removing seeds or nuts from their shells or pods.

specific_competence_name: Apply basic principles of husbandry in aquaculture production
learning_activity_name: Perform husbandry practices in aquaculture (fish, sea cucumber and seaweed farming)
sla_name: Husbandry practices in aquaculture
sla_assessment_criteria: Husbandry practices for aquaculture well carried out.
sla_teaching_aids: Production sites|Aquarium|Common tools/ equipment|Materials/ supplies used in aquaculture
sla_references: TET(2023), AGRICULTURE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students practise the routine management of fish, sea cucumber and seaweed farming.
sla_notes_details: Practices include preparing and fertilising ponds or sites, stocking, feeding and monitoring water quality, checking growth by sampling, controlling predators and diseases, harvesting and handling, and record keeping. Coastal practices include tying seaweed seedlings on lines or racks and monitoring their growth.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a sample of ten fish is weighed every two weeks to estimate average growth and adjust the feeding rate.
sla_notes_daily_life: These skills can be used to start small-scale fish or seaweed enterprises.
sla_exercise: Why is sampling done in a fish pond?::To estimate growth and adjust feeding.||How is seaweed commonly grown?::On lines or racks in shallow sea water.||Name one predator control measure in fish ponds.::Covering ponds with nets or fencing.

main_competence_name: Conduct a project in Agriculture
specific_competence_name: Carry out a project in Agriculture
learning_activity_name: Complete the crop/ animal-based production project started in Form III and submit a report
sla_name: Completing and reporting the agricultural production project
sla_assessment_criteria: The project started in Form III completed and a report submitted.
sla_teaching_aids: School farm / nearby farm enterprise|Tools equipment|Materials/ supplies appropriate to the project
sla_references: TET(2023), AGRICULTURE SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The project started in Form III is completed, evaluated and reported in Form IV.
sla_notes_details: Students complete production, harvest, market the produce, analyse costs and returns, evaluate the success and challenges and prepare a report. The report includes an introduction, objectives, methods, records, results, profit or loss, lessons learnt and recommendations, and is presented and submitted for assessment.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, profit is calculated as total revenue minus total costs; if revenue is 500,000 shillings and costs 350,000 shillings, the profit is 150,000 shillings.
sla_notes_daily_life: Completing and reporting projects prepares students for running real agricultural businesses.
sla_exercise: How is profit calculated?::Total revenue minus total costs.||Name one section of a project report.::Objectives (or methods, results, recommendations).||Why evaluate a project?::To learn lessons and improve future projects.
